analysis.one_liner: Requires corporations and LLCs to disclose their real owners to law enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill got no committee vote and no Senate vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require new and existing corporations and limited liability companies to file the names, birthdates, addresses, and ID numbers of their real owners with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which would share the information only with law enforcement. Today, a person can form a company in a U.S. state without ever identifying themselves, which is why criminals, corrupt foreign officials, and tax evaders use American shell companies to move money. The bill would close that gap, with civil and criminal penalties for filing false information, and would require federal contractors bidding on large contracts to disclose their owners. Exempted entities include large companies (over 20 employees and over $5 million in gross receipts), banks, insurers, and registered public companies, which already disclose ownership elsewhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit as victims of fraud, money laundering, and corruption that is harder to investigate when law enforcement cannot see who owns a company. Honest small businesses also benefit, because the bill directs Treasury to rewrite existing bank due-diligence rules to cut duplicative paperwork once a central owner registry exists [S3]. Law enforcement agencies gain a tool for detecting terrorism financing, money laundering, tax evasion, and other misconduct [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fraud victims, honest businesses, law enforcement

how_it_helps.text: Corporations and LLCs would have to file their beneficial owners' names, addresses, and ID numbers with FinCEN, giving police and prosecutors a way to find out who is behind a company used for crime [S2][S3].

False or incomplete owner filings would carry a civil penalty up to $10,000 and criminal penalties of up to three years in prison, and bearer shares — unregistered company certificates that hide who owns them — would be banned [S3].

The bill directs Treasury to revise existing bank due-diligence rules to reduce burdens on financial institutions that become unnecessary once a central registry exists, and funds FinCEN with up to $40 million from forfeiture funds [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of small companies — the bill exempts large firms, banks, insurers, and registered public companies, so the new annual filing falls mostly on smaller corporations and LLCs, which must submit personal identifying information to a federal database [S2][S3]. The interests that profit from corporate secrecy lose their product: the bill's stated purpose is to stop wrongdoers from exploiting U.S. companies for criminal gain [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Small-company owners; sellers of corporate secrecy

drawbacks.text: Millions of small corporations and LLCs would face a new filing requirement, submitting owners' personal information (name, birthdate, address, ID number) to FinCEN on an annual basis, with civil penalties up to $10,000 for willful failures [S2][S3].

Privacy critics worry about a federal database of personal identifiers, though the bill restricts disclosure to law-enforcement requests, foreign-agency requests under treaty, and financial institutions with customer consent, and only for law-enforcement, national security, or intelligence use [S3].

The exemptions are broad: companies with more than 20 employees and over $5 million in gross receipts, banks, insurers, registered public companies, and any class of business Treasury and the Attorney General jointly exempt are all off the hook, so large interests face little new burden while the smallest businesses comply [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — making shell companies traceable so fraud, laundering, and corruption can be prosecuted — is significant, and the bill tries to keep the cost down by exempting larger businesses and reimbursing FinCEN's compliance costs from forfeiture funds. The real burdens fall on small-company owners who must file, and on the secrecy industry, which loses its business model. The design is reasonable, though the asymmetric exemptions tilt compliance costs onto the smallest firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never voted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden introduced the bill on June 26, 2019, with Sens. Rubio and Whitehouse, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
The Senate Banking Committee took no further action: the complete action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote after the referral [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat, and never reached the Senate floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Whoever benefits from anonymous shell companies — the people and intermediaries that set them up — is better off that the bill died. Companies using U.S. entities to obscure ownership kept that ability through the 116th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anonymous shell-company users and secrecy intermediaries

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Transparency Act of 2019 and shepherded its referral to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it Republican support.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 26, 2019 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat leading with one Republican and one Democrat cosponsoring — but no committee or floor vote ever recorded who would have supported or opposed it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill attacks the product this business sells: companies whose real owners cannot be identified. Requiring owner disclosure to FinCEN removes the anonymity that customers of these services pay for, and the bill's stated purpose is to stop wrongdoers from exploiting U.S. companies for criminal gain [S3].

industries.industry: Individuals and networks using anonymous U.S. entities for laundering, tax evasion, or corruption
industries.note: U.S. companies can currently be formed without identifying the owner, making them a vehicle for moving illicit money; the bill would force disclosure with criminal penalties for false filings, directly threatening anyone relying on that secrecy [S3].

Banks currently must collect beneficial-ownership information under their own due-diligence rules; the bill directs Treasury to rewrite those rules to cut duplicative burdens once a central registry exists, and lets banks access registry data with customer consent. A modest gain wrapped in less paperwork.

Firms under the exemption thresholds (20 employees, $5 million in gross receipts) face new annual owner filings and penalties for willful failures, while their larger competitors are exempt. Honest small businesses gain somewhat from a financial system less prone to fraud, but they alone carry the compliance cost [S3].

Law enforcement agencies gain a registry they can query when investigating terrorism financing, money laundering, and fraud, funded by up to $40 million from Treasury and Justice forfeiture funds [S3].
